profiles.name: Larry Haines
profiles.excerpt: Larry Haines built one of radio's most prolific acting careers, moving from Gang Busters and starring detective roles to a major return on CBS Radio Mystery Theater decades later.
profiles.bio_html:
Larry Haines, born Larry Hecht in Mount Vernon, New York, entered broadcasting before television made him a familiar face. After developing an interest in acting in school and college, he passed a CBS audition and began working on small New York radio stations. Crime drama quickly became one of his specialties, and his early network work included Gang Busters.

Haines became a radio leading man as Joe Lincoln in Treasury Agent and later as Mike Hammer in That Hammer Guy, while also moving through anthology, mystery and serial programs. His long television run as Stu Bergman on Search for Tomorrow eventually overshadowed that microphone career in popular memory, but radio remained part of his professional life. In the 1970s he returned to the medium as a frequent performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 45 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances, 17 Inner Sanctum Mysteries appearances, eight each on The Shadow and Words at War, seven each on Gang Busters, Mr. Malone and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, plus six The Chase performances. The holdings span more than three decades of radio work.

profiles.name: Leon Janney
profiles.excerpt: Leon Janney grew from a child stage and radio performer into one of broadcasting's most versatile adult character actors, with a career that reached from early network drama to CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Leon Janney began performing as a child, appearing in vaudeville and onstage before entering radio in the 1920s. He also worked in films while young, but the microphone became one of the most durable parts of his career. As an adult he developed a reputation for character work and for the range of accents and dialects he could bring to radio drama.

That versatility kept Janney active across changing eras of broadcasting. His credits stretched through crime drama, science fiction and experimental radio, including Gang Busters, Dimension X, X Minus One, The Mysterious Traveler and CBS Radio Workshop. In the 1970s he became a recurring member of the CBS Radio Mystery Theater repertory, giving his career a late chapter in the revival of network radio drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 69 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances, nine each on The Chase and X Minus One, seven Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, five CBS Radio Workshop performances, four each on Dimension X and The Mysterious Traveler, and three Theater Five appearances.

profiles.name: Mercedes McCambridge
profiles.excerpt: Mercedes McCambridge was a radio actress before she was an Oscar winner, using a remarkably flexible voice across I Love a Mystery, Inner Sanctum and later CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Mercedes McCambridge began professional radio work while studying English and theater in Chicago, where NBC recognized her talent and signed her to a long-term contract. The medium became the foundation of her career. Her voice could move between sharply different ages, personalities and accents, and she became especially valuable in repertory drama where one actor might be asked to create several distinct people in a single story.

I Love a Mystery showed that flexibility particularly well. McCambridge later recalled playing multiple women within the same serial, sometimes arguing with one another in the same episode. She also worked on Inner Sanctum, Lights Out, Gang Busters and many other programs, and starred as attorney Martha Ellis Bryan in Defense Attorney. Film brought her an Academy Award for All the King's Men, and decades later her radio-honed vocal control contributed to the demon voice in The Exorcist.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 67 I Love a Mystery performances, 22 CBS Radio Mystery Theater appearances, 19 Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances, eight Lights Out appearances, three Gang Busters episodes and additional work on Screen Directors Playhouse, Suspense and The Great Gildersleeve.

profiles.name: Peggy Webber
profiles.excerpt: Peggy Webber spent nearly nine decades treating radio as a living dramatic art, first as a highly versatile network actress and later as the founder, writer, producer and director behind California Artists Radio Theatre.
profiles.bio_html:
Peggy Webber began performing before she was old enough for school and entered radio as a child. By the 1940s she had become a remarkably flexible microphone actress, capable of shifting age, accent and character quickly enough to play multiple parts in the same production. Her radio work placed her beside directors and writers including Orson Welles, Norman Corwin and Jack Webb, while film and television added another layer to a career that always kept returning to sound drama.

Webber did more than perform. She wrote, adapted, produced and directed, and in 1984 founded California Artists Radio Theatre to keep professionally produced radio drama alive. CART mounted classic and contemporary works with veteran actors and distributed productions through public radio. Webber remained its central producer and director, supervising adaptations, music and editing. She died in August 2026 at age 100 after a career in which preserving the craft of radio theater became a major part of her legacy.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Sears Radio Theater performances, 18 Escape appearances, 16 Broadway Is My Beat episodes, 13 This Is Your FBI performances, ten Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances and additional work on Have Gun, Will Travel, Tales of the Texas Rangers and A Man Called X.

profiles.name: Marian Seldes
profiles.excerpt: Marian Seldes brought the discipline of one of America's great stage careers into radio, becoming a defining repertory voice of CBS Radio Mystery Theater during the 1970s and early 1980s.
profiles.bio_html:
Marian Seldes trained for the stage and made her Broadway debut in 1948, beginning a career that eventually brought her a Tony Award, multiple further nominations and a reputation for extraordinary theatrical discipline. She studied with teachers including Sanford Meisner, Katharine Cornell and Martha Graham and later taught generations of actors at Juilliard.

Radio was another serious acting space for Seldes rather than a novelty beside Broadway. When Himan Brown's CBS Radio Mystery Theater restored network dramatic radio in 1974, Seldes became one of the voices most closely associated with its repertory company. Across horror, mystery and psychological drama, the series gave her repeated opportunities to build characters using only voice and timing.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 125 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances by Seldes, spanning from 1974 through 1981. That concentrated run makes her one of the largest single-series actor holdings in GRH's people index and an important bridge between classic network radio technique and the medium's 1970s revival.

profiles.name: Al Hodge
profiles.excerpt: Al Hodge originated Britt Reid on The Green Hornet and was also part of the WXYZ production machinery behind the station's adventure dramas before television made him famous as Captain Video.
profiles.bio_html:
Albert Hodge came to radio after studying drama at Miami University in Ohio and touring with a theatrical company. WXYZ in Detroit gave him a place to use more than his acting voice. He originated Britt Reid, the newspaper publisher who became the Green Hornet, and played the role through the program's formative years, helping establish one of radio's most recognizable masked heroes.

Hodge also worked behind the microphone. At WXYZ he wrote and announced, handled production duties and helped produce radio drama and documentary programming. Surviving Lone Ranger documentation also credits him as a director. After radio, Hodge became nationally known as the title hero of television's Captain Video and His Video Rangers, but the earlier WXYZ years show an actor who also understood how serial broadcasting was built.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 98 The Green Hornet episodes crediting Hodge, 20 The Lone Ranger appearances and individual performances on Boston Blackie, Columbia Workshop, Gang Busters, Gunsmoke and Theater Five. His verified production and directing work makes Directors, Producers & Editors a legitimate secondary GRH category.

profiles.name: Ted de Corsia
profiles.excerpt: Ted de Corsia's hard-edged screen villains grew out of a long radio apprenticeship in which his deep, forceful voice moved through The Shadow, Ellery Queen, Richard Diamond and scores of network dramas.
profiles.bio_html:
Ted de Corsia was a radio actor before Hollywood discovered how effectively his voice and physical presence could suggest danger. He began working in broadcasting in New York during the early network era and became a regular dramatic performer, with assignments ranging from impersonations on The March of Time to Sergeant Velie on The Adventures of Ellery Queen.

Crime drama suited de Corsia particularly well, but radio gave him more range than his later film image as a gangster or heavy might suggest. He worked on The Shadow, Gang Busters, Escape, Richard Diamond, Private Detective, This Is Your FBI and many anthology programs. On Richard Diamond he briefly stepped into the recurring role of Lieutenant Levinson before Arthur Q. Bryan took over. His later film career, beginning with Orson Welles' The Lady from Shanghai, carried the same commanding vocal presence to the screen.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 Richard Diamond, Private Detective performances, 15 This Is Your FBI appearances, 12 Escape episodes, 11 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances, nine The Shadow appearances, seven Columbia Workshop episodes and additional work on Let George Do It and Suspense.

profiles.name: Santos Ortega
profiles.excerpt: Santos Ortega was one of New York radio's great character actors, equally at home as Commissioner Weston on The Shadow, Inspector Queen, Nero Wolfe, Charlie Chan and the stock company of Inner Sanctum.
profiles.bio_html:
Santos Ortega entered radio during its early growth and learned quickly that vocal flexibility could create a career. Born in New York City to a Spanish father and Irish mother, he developed dialect work and character technique that opened a wide range of parts. Comedy led into drama, and by the network era he had become one of the medium's most dependable voices.

Ortega's continuing roles alone show remarkable range. He originated Inspector Richard Queen on The Adventures of Ellery Queen, played Commissioner Weston on The Shadow, starred at different times as Nero Wolfe, Bulldog Drummond and Charlie Chan, and worked steadily in daytime serials. He was also one of the New York stock actors who returned week after week to Inner Sanctum Mysteries and other anthologies, often disappearing into a new identity each broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 53 Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances, 19 The Shadow appearances, 11 X Minus One episodes, eight Columbia Workshop performances, seven Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances and additional work on Barrie Craig, CBS Radio Mystery Theater and The Mysterious Traveler.

profiles.name: Elaine Alpert
profiles.excerpt: Elaine Alpert was a long-serving member of The Lone Ranger's WXYZ repertory company, one of the recurring supporting actors who supplied new frontier characters across hundreds of serialized broadcasts.
profiles.bio_html:
Elaine Alpert is one of the radio professionals whose work survives more clearly than her personal publicity. She belonged to the Detroit-area repertory surrounding WXYZ's The Lone Ranger, where supporting actors had to create a continuing stream of townspeople, victims, relatives and other story characters around Brace Beemer's Ranger and John Todd's Tonto.

Surviving cast documentation places Alpert inside that company during the 1940s, and later episode records continue to credit her as the serial moved through the postwar years. The value of that work was consistency without sameness: a repertory actor could return repeatedly while sounding like the new character a script required rather than like a permanent member of the cast.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies 113 The Lone Ranger performances credited to Alpert, spanning broadcasts from 1941 through 1956. With personal biographical documentation limited, that sustained record is the proper center of her GRH profile and preserves her place in the production system behind one of radio's longest-running adventure series.

profiles.name: Harry Goldstein
profiles.excerpt: Harry Goldstein left Detroit public-school teaching for a freelance radio career, becoming a familiar WXYZ repertory voice on The Lone Ranger and Challenge of the Yukon.
profiles.bio_html:
Harry Goldstein entered radio while he was still a senior at Wayne State University and teaching in the Detroit public schools. The school schedule left room for acting assignments, and radio soon paid better than teaching. What began as part-time microphone work became a freelance profession in the same Detroit broadcasting world that produced The Lone Ranger, The Green Hornet and Challenge of the Yukon.

Goldstein later remembered the precision demanded by live and transcribed radio drama. Programs were timed tightly, leaving little room for improvisation, and repertory actors learned to shape a character while also landing every scene on schedule. On WXYZ's adventure shows, Goldstein became one of the recurring supporting voices who could be assigned a different part from story to story without disturbing the identity of the continuing heroes.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 109 The Lone Ranger performances and three Challenge of the Yukon appearances credited to Goldstein. Surviving episode documentation places him alongside performers such as Brace Beemer, John Todd, Paul Hughes, Rollon Parker and Bill Saunders, confirming his place in the WXYZ repertory system.
